If you want to study an undergraduate course in the UK, you will probably need UCAS.

The short answer is simple: to apply to UCAS, create a UCAS Hub account, choose your course options, complete your personal and education details, add your personal statement and reference, pay the UCAS application fee, and submit your application before the deadline.

That is the clean version.

This guide explains how to apply through UCAS for 2027 entry, especially for international students who want to study in the UK.

If you are still comparing countries or courses, first understand how planning a UK undergraduate journey works before you finalise your UCAS choices.

What Is UCAS?

UCAS means the Universities and Colleges Admissions Service. It is the central application system for most UK undergraduate university and college courses.

Instead of applying separately to several universities, you can apply through UCAS and send one application to up to five course choices. Universities then review your UCAS application and send their decisions through your UCAS account.

You start the process from the official UCAS Hub. From there, you can register, fill in your UCAS application form, track university decisions and reply to offers.

Here’s the thing: UCAS makes the application process easier, but it does not choose the right course for you. That part still needs research, planning and a realistic shortlist.

Key UCAS Dates for 2027 Entry

UCAS dates change by year, so always check the official UCAS dates and deadlines before you submit.

For 2027 entry, these are the important dates:

UCAS stage

Date

2027 course search opens

28 April 2026

UCAS applications open

12 May 2026

Completed applications can be submitted

1 September 2026

Oxford, Cambridge, medicine, dentistry and veterinary deadline

15 October 2026, 18:00 UK time

Equal consideration deadline for most undergraduate courses

13 January 2027, 18:00 UK time

Applications after 30 June 2027

Usually enter Clearing

Final date for 2027 entry applications

23 September 2027, 18:00 UK time

The equal consideration deadline means universities should consider all applications received by that date equally. You can still apply after the deadline if courses remain open, but your chance may depend on available places.

How Much Is The UCAS Application Fee?

For the 2027 cycle, the official UCAS application fee is £34.50. This fee allows you to add up to five university or college choices to your undergraduate application.

For rough planning, UCAS says international students may pay around £11,000 per year in tuition fees, while some courses can cost around £30,000 per year. Living expenses may be around £8,000 to £11,000 per year, depending on your city, lifestyle and accommodation.

What You Need Before Starting Your UCAS Application

Do not open the UCAS application form and start guessing. Prepare the essentials first.

Information or document

Why it matters

Passport details

Helps match your identity and international applicant record

Academic certificates or transcripts

Shows completed qualifications

Predicted grades

Needed if you are still studying

English language evidence

Course shortlist

Helps you choose up to five courses wisely

Personal statement answers

Shows your course motivation and preparation

Academic reference

Supports your ability, attitude and predicted performance

Payment card

Needed to pay the UCAS application fee

How To Apply Through UCAS Step by Step

The UCAS application form has several sections. Work through them slowly and save your progress as you go.

1. Register In The UCAS Hub

Go to the UCAS website and create your UCAS Hub account. Choose the correct entry year and select undergraduate study.

Use a personal email address that you check regularly. Do not use a school email if you may lose access after graduation. UCAS and universities may send important updates there.

This is your UCAS registration stage. Keep your login details safe.

2. Start Your UCAS Application

After registration, open your UCAS Hub dashboard and start the application. UCAS will ask for your personal details, contact details, nationality, residency status and background information.

3. Add Nationality, Residency And Finance Details

International students should take this section seriously. UCAS may ask where you were born, where you live, your nationality and your residency history.

Do not confuse nationality with residency. They are not always the same.

4. Add Your Education History

Enter your completed and pending qualifications. This may include A Levels, International Baccalaureate, HSC, CBSE, ISC, WAEC, NECO, foundation courses or other national qualifications.

Do not translate grades casually by yourself. Choose the qualification names in UCAS as accurately as possible. If your results are pending, your school, college or referee may add predicted grades.

Some courses also require admissions tests. Medicine, dentistry, veterinary medicine, law, maths, engineering and Oxbridge courses may need tests such as UCAT, LNAT, MAT, TMUA or other assessments.

5. Add Employment Or Work Experience

UCAS includes a section for paid work experience. Add relevant employment if you have it.

No paid work? That is not a disaster. Use your personal statement to explain volunteering, shadowing, projects, competitions, wider reading or practical experience linked to your chosen subject.

Specific evidence beats broad claims. A nursing applicant can mention care exposure. A computing applicant can mention a coding project. A business applicant can mention a small sales project, family business task or market research activity.

6. Choose Up To Five Courses

Most undergraduate applicants can choose up to five courses through UCAS. They can be at different universities or sometimes different courses at the same university.

Medicine, dentistry and veterinary medicine usually allow up to four choices in those subjects. Oxford and Cambridge also have special restrictions, so check before applying.

Think about your five choices this way:

  • one or two ambitious choices
  • two or three realistic choices
  • one safer choice where your grades clearly match the entry requirements

The surprising part? The “safe” choice is not always the lowest-ranked university. It is the course where your grades, English level, subject background, budget and career plan fit best.

Before you submit, make sure you understand how your five choices should work.

7. Write Your UCAS Personal Statement

For 2026 entry onwards, UCAS changed the personal statement format. Applicants now answer three structured questions instead of writing only one open essay.

The official UCAS personal statement guidance focuses on:

  1. Why do you want to study this course or subject?
  2. How have your qualifications and studies helped you prepare?
  3. What else have you done outside education to prepare, and why is it useful?

The total limit is still 4,000 characters, including spaces. UCAS says admissions staff will review the answers as one personal statement.

This structure helps international students because it pushes you to be specific. Do not simply say, “I am passionate about business.” Show where that interest came from. Maybe you helped with pricing in a family business, studied economics, joined a school enterprise project or worked with customers.

If you are applying for law, connect your interest to reading, debate, social issues, legal systems or work shadowing. If you are applying for computer science, mention maths, coding, problem-solving or a real project you tried.

For extra writing clarity, you can use this guide on shaping academic motivation, but keep your final UCAS personal statement aligned with UCAS rules.

8. Add Your Academic Reference

Your UCAS application needs a reference. This usually comes from a teacher, tutor, counsellor or academic adviser who knows your ability and study habits.

Give your referee time. Share your course list, predicted grades, achievements, subject interests and any important context. A rushed reference can weaken an otherwise strong application.

9. Review, Pay And Submit

Before paying, check everything.

Look at your name, date of birth, email, course codes, campus codes, qualification details, predicted grades, personal statement and reference status.

Then pay the UCAS application fee and submit. For 2027 entry, the UCAS application fee is £34.50.

Once submitted, UCAS sends your application to your chosen universities and colleges.

What Happens After You Submit Your UCAS Application?

After submission, universities review your application and respond through UCAS.

You may receive:

  • a conditional offer
  • an unconditional offer
  • an interview invitation
  • a portfolio request
  • a test request
  • a request for extra documents
  • an unsuccessful decision

Before replying, understand what different offer types mean. Your firm and insurance choices can affect your next steps.

UCAS Extra And Clearing

UCAS Extra is for applicants who used all five choices and are not holding any offers. It lets you add another choice, one at a time, if you are eligible.

Clearing is different. It helps students find available courses later in the cycle. You may use Clearing if you applied late, missed offer conditions, changed your mind or received no offers.

Do not treat Clearing as failure. Many students use it well.

Notes For International Students By Country

This section is not about creating separate country pages. It is here because students from different countries prepare different qualifications and documents.

India: Check whether your chosen course accepts CBSE, ISC, state board, A Level or foundation qualifications. Some universities may ask for subject-specific marks, especially for engineering, computing, health and business courses.

Pakistan: Prepare HSSC, A Level or other qualification details accurately. Competitive subjects may require tests, interviews or stronger predicted grades.

Nigeria: WAEC, NECO, A Level and foundation routes can differ by university. Some courses also ask for specific English or subject requirements, so check each course page before adding it to UCAS.

Nepal and Sri Lanka: Pay close attention to transcript format, English evidence and predicted grades if you are still studying. Universities may assess qualifications differently by course.

United States: UCAS is different from the Common App. You usually write one UK-style personal statement for all choices, and your academic subject focus matters more than broad extracurricular storytelling.

Common UCAS Application Mistakes

Students often make UCAS harder than it needs to be.

They choose five unrelated courses and then struggle to write one personal statement that fits all of them. They miss the October deadline for medicine, dentistry, veterinary medicine, Oxford or Cambridge. They enter qualification names incorrectly. They wait too long to ask for a reference.

Another common mistake is checking only university ranking. Ranking matters, but fit matters more. A course with the right entry requirements, location, tuition fee, support and career route can be a smarter choice than a famous name that does not suit your profile.

If English is your main concern, compare how UK universities set English requirements before you apply.

Quick UCAS Application Checklist

Before submitting your UCAS application, check:

Checklist item

Status

Correct entry year selected

  

UCAS Hub account created

  

Course codes checked

  

Campus codes checked

  

Qualification names and grades checked

  

Predicted grades added if needed

  

Personal statement answers complete

  

Academic reference ready

  

English requirements reviewed

  

UCAS application fee ready

  

Passport and personal details checked

  

Tuition and living costs reviewed

  
 

A strong UCAS application is not always dramatic. It is accurate, focused and submitted on time.

FAQs About UCAS Applications

How do I apply to UCAS?

You apply to UCAS by creating a UCAS Hub account, starting an undergraduate application, adding personal details, education history, course choices, a personal statement and a reference, then paying the UCAS application fee and submitting before the deadline.

How do international students apply through UCAS?

What is the UCAS application form?

The UCAS application form is the online form inside UCAS Hub. It collects your personal details, education history, employment information, course choices, personal statement, reference and payment.

How many courses can I apply to through UCAS?

Most undergraduate applicants can apply to up to five courses. Medicine, dentistry and veterinary medicine usually allow up to four choices in those subjects.

What is the UCAS application fee for 2027?

The official UCAS application fee for the 2027 cycle is £34.50. This covers up to five university or college choices.

What is the UCAS deadline for 2027 entry?

For most undergraduate courses, the equal consideration deadline is 13 January 2027 at 18:00 UK time. Oxford, Cambridge, medicine, dentistry and veterinary medicine usually have an earlier 15 October 2026 deadline.

Do I need IELTS before applying to UCAS?

Not always. Some universities allow you to apply before your final English test result and may give you a conditional offer requiring a specific score later. Check each university’s course page.

Can I apply to UCAS without final grades?

Yes. Many students apply with pending qualifications. Your school, college or referee may provide predicted grades.

What happens if I get no UCAS offers?

You may be able to use UCAS Extra if you used all five choices and hold no offers. Later in the cycle, Clearing may also help you find available courses.

Can I change my UCAS choices after submitting?

UCAS allows some changes within limited timeframes and conditions. After that, changes may be restricted, so check your course choices carefully before submitting.

Final Thoughts

Applying to UCAS is not difficult when you understand the steps. The real challenge is making the right choices before you submit.

For 2027 entry, start early, check the official UCAS deadlines, prepare your documents carefully and choose courses that match your academic profile and long-term goals. A focused application is always stronger than a rushed one.
